title: Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host
content:
1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

Supervision architecture and its fit to the science. FIELDWISE is a European Postdoctoral Fellowship carried out by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE). It is supervised at the host by Prof. András Jung, with Dr. Roland Hollós as co-supervisor. The supervision is deliberately two-headed because the project's scientific problem sits precisely on the boundary between plant biology and geospatial data science, and no single supervisor spans both the Earth-observation and the machine-learning methodology the action requires. Prof. András Jung is a Professor at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose research field is remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy — the exact disciplines that make hypothesis H2 (hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer) and the satellite-scaling design testable. Dr. Roland Hollós is based in ELTE's Department of Meteorology and works on machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and agro-meteorology; he provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing, i.e. for the prospective, uncertainty-aware prediction of WP3 Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction and the cross-country adaptation methods of WP4 Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability, while the fellow designs, builds and runs the models. The division of supervisory responsibility therefore maps one-to-one onto the two methodological pillars of the proposal rather than being a nominal co-supervision.

Qualifications and track record of the supervisors. The supervisory team's standing is evidenced by an active, recent and directly relevant publication record. Prof. András Jung's recent output includes peer-reviewed articles in remote sensing and agricultural Earth observation — among them work on agricultural lighting and Daily Light Integral mapping (Agronomy, 2025; Applied Sciences, 2025), remote-sensing monitoring of agricultural land-use intensity (Agriculture, 2025) and a methodological contribution on vectorising building structures (IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters, 2024) that evidences the breadth of his remote-sensing methods. This body of work substantiates the host-side expertise the fellow will draw on and confirms that the supervisor leads an active EO/hyperspectral research programme at professorial level. Dr. Roland Hollós's methodological standing is evidenced by his machine-learning and meta-modelling work, including a 2026 contribution in Geoscientific Model Development, which is directly pertinent to the Bayesian/hierarchical modelling and uncertainty-quantification methods he will quality-assure. The supervision is anchored in the host's own experimental infrastructure — the Institute's GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory holds hyperspectral instrumentation (an Ultris S5 and a Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite package), UAV payloads, licensed geospatial and numerical software, and high-performance computing with secure storage — so advanced training is delivered against real equipment and data rather than in the abstract. Prof. András Jung chairs the Project Steering Group and is the standing escalation point for scientific and training matters, which places the most senior supervisory authority at the centre of the governance model.

Supervision quality: cadence, governance and decision rights. Supervision quality is made concrete through an explicit, agreed cadence rather than left to good intention. The fellow and the supervisor hold a weekly one-to-one meeting; a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor runs through the WP3 and WP4 modelling and transferability phase, tapering to monthly outside that window, so intensive methodological support is concentrated where the modelling and cross-country work is most demanding. A monthly written progress record is held by the fellow, and a quarterly review is conducted against the Career Development Plan with both supervisors present. Oversight is exercised by a Project Steering Group chaired by the supervisor, comprising the fellow, the co-supervisor and one named contact each from the three associated organisations (Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság), which issues a go/no-go verdict on the project milestones MS1 to MS5. Decision rights are allocated without overlap: scientific method and day-to-day research choices rest with the fellow (escalating to the supervisor); the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing rest with the co-supervisor (escalating to the supervisor); the training plan, resources and milestone go/no-go recommendation rest with the supervisor (escalating to the Steering Group); and contract, finance, IP and open-access policy rest with the host. The committed supervisory effort is planned as an in-kind contribution of the order of 2.5 person-months from the supervisor and 2.0 person-months from the co-supervisor across the action, built bottom-up from this governance. This design directly serves the call's expected outcome of enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision at the participating organisation.

The Career Development Plan as the training instrument. Training is organised through a Career Development Plan, delivered as an early project deliverable, D1.3 Career Development Plan, due in month 3, owned by the fellow and the supervisor and established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher; with a co-supervisor in place, joint establishment means the plan is signed by both supervisors and the fellow. This satisfies the instrument's mandatory requirement that a Career Development Plan covering research objectives, training and career needs, transferable skills, teaching, publications and Open Science be agreed jointly and submitted at the start of the action. The plan is agreed by month 3 and reviewed at five points — at months 6, 12, 16, 20 and 27 — alongside the governance decision points, with the month-27 review falling inside the placement, when non-academic career development is most in play. Its six components are: the research objectives O1 to O6; training and career needs; transferable skills; teaching; publications planning; and Open Science engagement.

Planned training activities: scientific, management and transferable skills. Scientific training is delivered as eleven host-to-fellow competences (below), through supervised research practice combined with named ELTE courses, and structured around the fellow's intended progression from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. It closes the fellow's specific competence gap in Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation and decision evaluation. Transferable-skill training is carried as seven explicit strands of the plan: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication — directly meeting the call's requirement that training integrate key transferable and digital skills (including generative AI), foster an Open Science culture and good scientific conduct including research integrity. Management and project-leadership training is embedded in the fellow's ownership of the monthly progress record, her scientific-method decision rights, her responsibility for grant-writing and exploitation strands, and her seat on the Steering Group. Research-integrity and open-science competence are trained and evidenced rather than merely asserted: FIELDWISE follows "as open as possible, as closed as necessary", and the plan commits the fellow to open-access publication, code and model cards where IP permits, FAIR metadata and validation split manifests. Publications planning targets four principal scientific outputs (P1 physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures; P2 hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling; P3 temporal and cross-country transferability; P4 research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation), with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, plus one public field demonstration with commercial growers and one public-facing article per year for public engagement.

Teaching and feedback of research into education. The teaching component is framed not as a competence to be acquired but as an existing strength transferred to a new discipline, institution and language of instruction: the fellow taught for five years at Agricultural University - Plovdiv (2015-2020), including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English and Bachelor's thesis supervision. The developmental content is the move from plant-protection teaching in Bulgarian at an agricultural university to Earth-observation teaching in English at an informatics faculty, and the step up to doctoral-level supervision. Two concrete measures carry it: co-designing and delivering a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture (rather than a single guest lecture), and co-supervising the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. This feeds research results back into teaching at the host, meeting the corresponding expected outcome.

Two-way transfer of knowledge between researcher and host (European Fellowship). Because FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship, the relevant knowledge transfer is the two-way exchange between the researcher and the host; the three-way transfer required only for the outgoing phase of a Global Fellowship does not apply. The exchange is genuinely bidirectional and is specified in both directions. From the host to the fellow: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research-software and web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. From the fellow to the host: plant physiology; horticultural crop science; plant protection and agronomy; water-stress experimentation; physiological phenotyping; hyperspectral field measurement; biological interpretation of EO; the preliminary DrR - Digital Agronomist development; and access to complementary agricultural research collaborations. This transfer is not a side benefit but the mechanism of the science: it is what allows spectral observations to be anchored to physiological meaning and machine-learned relationships to be interpreted as crop-water processes rather than black-box correlations, so the physiological-target and transferability objectives depend on the exchange working in both directions. The exchange is completed into an academic-research-industry knowledge chain by the associated organisations — Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem supplies the long-term experimental knowledge and source-domain dataset for model development and validation, Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив supplies the independent Bulgarian research environment for cross-country scientific transferability (a Hungary-to-Bulgaria test rather than a mere increase in sample size), and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság supplies the bridge from research field to farmer field and from research prototype to operational requirements.

Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement. AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság is the non-academic placement host, and the fellowship includes a six-month placement at the end of the action (M25-M30, in Budaörs), following the 24-month research fellowship at ELTE (M1-M24); it is an integral, evaluated part of the proposal, not an add-on. Its added value for the project is that it makes the operational-transfer half of FIELDWISE structural rather than asserted: gap G5 and hypothesis H5 both claim that research-to-farm transfer is where models break, and a six-month period embedded inside the company that runs the commercial farms is the strongest available evidence that the project takes its own hardest gap seriously; it also directly answers the prior-evaluation criticism that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated. Its added value for the researcher's career is the inter-sectoral half of her progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide, and which is precisely the segment of profile that makes her employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia, realising the call's inter-sectoral employability outcome. The placement must sit inside the company and needs its full six months because its work content depends on the company's own operational environment: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing D5.4 AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (due in month 30); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company, producing D5.5 FMIS integration roadmap (due in month 30); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság co-leads WP5 Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP and hosts the fellow for the placement, which is scheduled after the web MVP has already been built so that the placement is validation and transfer rather than first build. On the current record the placement is planned to be supervised on site by a named senior member of staff at senior research grade, working with the company's product-development team responsible for its farm management information system, with access to a desk or office and to the FMIS development/staging and customer-data environments; these placement-host arrangements are operator-provided working assumptions to be confirmed with the company before the placement begins, but the placement's structure, work content and evaluated deliverables are fixed by the design. An in-kind commitment of the order of 3.0 person-months from the placement host is planned, the largest partner figure precisely because it is the only partner hosting the fellow. In sum, the supervision is expert and role-matched, the training is comprehensive and instrument-compliant, the knowledge transfer is demonstrably two-way and load-bearing for the science, and the non-academic placement converts the proposal's most demanding claim into structural evidence while completing the fellow's inter-sectoral profile.

claim_statuses.claim_summary: The fellow is Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, a plant physiologist carrying out a European Postdoctoral Fellowship, with five years of prior teaching at Agricultural University - Plovdiv (2015-2020).
The host is Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics.

The supervisor is Prof. András Jung, a Professor at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose field is remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and who chairs the Steering Group and is the escalation point.

The co-supervisor is Dr. Roland Hollós, ELTE Department of Meteorology, working on machine learning and meta-modelling; he provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing.

Prof. András Jung's recent peer-reviewed publications (Agronomy 2025; Applied Sciences 2025; Agriculture 2025; IEEE GRSL 2024) evidence an active professorial-level EO/hyperspectral research programme.
Dr. Roland Hollós's machine-learning and meta-modelling standing is evidenced by a 2026 Geoscientific Model Development contribution relevant to the methods he quality-assures.

The host Institute's GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory holds hyperspectral instrumentation (Ultris S5, Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite), UAV payloads, licensed geospatial/numerical software and HPC with secure storage, against which advanced training is delivered.
FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship, so two-way researcher-host transfer applies and the Global Fellowship three-way transfer does not.
The action runs 30 months: a 24-month European Fellowship at ELTE (M1-M24) plus a 6-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25-M30).

Training is organised through a Career Development Plan delivered as D1.3 Career Development Plan due in month 3, owned by the fellow and supervisor, established jointly and signed by both supervisors and the fellow.
The plan's six components are research objectives O1-O6, training and career needs, transferable skills, teaching, publications planning, and Open Science engagement.
The Career Development Plan is agreed by month 3 and reviewed at five points: months 6, 12, 16, 20 and 27, with the month-27 review inside the placement.
Scientific training is delivered as eleven host-to-fellow competences through supervised practice plus named ELTE courses.

Transferable-skill training is carried as seven strands: research integrity, open science and FAIR practice, generative-AI literacy, grant writing, IP and exploitation, project management, and science communication.

Training is structured around the fellow's progression from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to independent researcher, closing a competence gap in Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation.

Open-science competence is trained and evidenced through open-access publication, code and model cards where IP permits, FAIR metadata and validation split manifests, following the principle of as open as possible, as closed as necessary.

Publications planning targets four scientific outputs P1-P4 with at least two peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, plus one public field demonstration and one public-facing article per year.

Supervision cadence: weekly one-to-one fellow-supervisor meeting; weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through the WP3/WP4 phase tapering to monthly; monthly written progress record; quarterly Career Development Plan review with both supervisors.
A Project Steering Group chaired by the supervisor, with the fellow, the co-supervisor and one named contact each from MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR, issues go/no-go verdicts on milestones MS1 to MS5.
Decision rights are allocated without overlap across fellow, co-supervisor, supervisor and host.

Host-to-fellow transfer covers geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, optical/SAR integration, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal and Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning/domain adaptation, reproducible geospatial computation, research-software/web deployment, and IP/exploitation.

Fellow-to-host transfer covers plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection/agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement, biological interpretation of EO, DrR preliminary development, and access to complementary agricultural collaborations.

The transfer is genuinely bidirectional (crop physiology/agronomy <-> geospatial/data science) and is the mechanism by which spectral observations are anchored to physiological meaning, forming an academic-research-industry knowledge chain with MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR.

Teaching feeds research into education via two measures: co-designing and delivering a full module unit in an ELTE MSc Earth-observation-for-agriculture course, and co-supervising the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work; framed as an existing teaching strength transferred to a new discipline, institution and language.

The AgroVIR non-academic placement (six months, M25-M30, Budaörs) makes the operational-transfer half structural (G5/H5), answers prior-evaluation criticism on the route to users, and supplies the inter-sectoral half of the fellow's career progression; its work content depends on the company's operational environment.

Placement work content comprises operational hardening in a production FMIS environment, the nine-dimension operational assessment producing D5.4 AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (due month 30), the FMIS integration roadmap producing D5.5 FMIS integration roadmap (due month 30), and requirements engineering/user testing with commercial growers; AgroVIR co-leads WP5 and hosts the fellow, with D5.1 built before the placement.
Miklós Maróti
Senior research officer
The AgroVIR product development team responsible for the FMIS platform.
Desk or office space at AgroVIR for M25-M30, access to the FMIS development and staging environment, and access to the customer-data environment.

The training and supervision design serves the call's expected outcomes and scope requirements on transferable/digital skills, Open Science and research integrity (SR-04), the joint Career Development Plan (SR-05), the evaluated non-academic placement (SR-06), and enhanced training/supervision quality and feedback into teaching (EO-05, EO-08).
